title: DiscoveryDocument
description: The OpenID Provider metadata document served at /.well-known/openid-configuration, derived from identity_oidc::discovery::DiscoveryDocument. Every field is a PROMISE. Promising a response type or grant the implementation does not serve is how a conformance suite fails and how a client picks an endpoint that will 501. In the bootstrap phase the document is CONSTRUCTIBLE (DiscoveryDocument::bootstrap) but the ROUTE that serves it is DEFERRED to phase 4, so no client can fetch it: a document that is right and unreachable is still unreachable.
x-serde-status: the document is IMPLEMENTED as a shape — DiscoveryDocument::bootstrap is a real function and a real test; the /.well-known/openid-configuration route is DEFERRED to phase 4 (OIDC provider)

issuer.description: The issuer identifier. Every token this provider mints carries an iss that must equal this string exactly, including scheme and any trailing slash. Not a URL this provider resolves.
issuer.x-construction: the argument to DiscoveryDocument::bootstrap; every endpoint below is derived from it by string concatenation

jwks_uri.description: The JWKS URI — the public keys clients use to verify this provider's signatures.

scopes_supported.description: The scopes this provider supports. The openid scope is mandatory for an OIDC provider and is not optional here.

x-accepted-values.constraining: the field is a Vec<String> in Rust; a provider without the openid scope is not an OIDC provider

response_types_supported.description: The response types this provider supports. 'code' only: the implicit and hybrid flows return tokens in a redirect, and a token in a URL is a token in a browser history, a referrer header and a proxy log.

grant_types_supported.description: The grant types this provider supports. authorization_code and refresh_token; never implicit, never password. The token endpoint's TokenRequest::grant maps anything else to Unsupported, so advertising a third value would be advertising a 501.

x-accepted-values.source: DiscoveryDocument::bootstrap, cross-checked against TokenRequest::grant which recognises exactly these two

subject_types_supported.description: The subject identifier types. 'public' only — the same subject for the same user across every client, which is the privacy-preserving choice. 'pairwise' would be the stronger privacy property and is NOT this provider's: advertising it without implementing it would be a lie clients act on.

id_token_signing_alg_values_supported.description: The signing algorithms this provider's ID tokens may be signed with. RS256 only.

userinfo_signing_alg_values_supported.description: The signing algorithms this provider's userinfo responses may use. RS256 only, even though UserInfoResponse is an unsigned JSON document by design — the field is declared because a signed userinfo response is specified and some clients require it. A client seeing this may attempt to fetch a signed userinfo response; this provider does not produce one.
userinfo_signing_alg_values_supported.x-divergence-from-code: The discovery document advertises RS256 for userinfo while identity_oidc::response::UserInfoResponse is an unsigned JSON document. Both are true as written: the advertisement is a capability declaration, and no route produces a signed userinfo response. A client that requires a signed userinfo response is not one this provider serves.

code_challenge_methods_supported.description: The PKCE code-challenge methods. S256 only. 'plain' is not advertised: declaring a downgrade offer is worse than advertising the weak one, and advertising both is worse than advertising one.

x-accepted-values.source: identity_oidc::SUPPORTED_CODE_CHALLENGE_METHOD; AuthorizationRequest::uses_supported_pkce checks against the same constant

token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported.description: The token endpoint's client authentication methods. client_secret_basic and client_secret_post for confidential clients, none for public ones. private_key_jwt is NOT offered, even though ClientMetadata carries a jwks_uri field: a client that offers one is offering something the token endpoint will not accept, and the discovery document is where the refusal is visible.

x-accepted-values.source: DiscoveryDocument::bootstrap, which writes these three; identity_oidc::client::ClientMetadata::SUPPORTED_AUTH_METHODS declares the identical set

claims_supported.description: The claims this provider may put in an ID token. The first twelve are the registered and this-provider's own claims IdTokenClaims always or conditionally carries; email_verified is the last.

x-accepted-values.source: DiscoveryDocument::bootstrap — the twelve names, in that order
x-accepted-values.cross-check: the eight required claims of IdTokenClaims plus the three optional profile/email claims; nonce is a registered claim that may be null

claims_parameter_supported.description: Whether this provider accepts the 'claims' request parameter. Declined explicitly as false rather than omitted: absent means 'unspecified', and a client that reads unspecified as 'maybe' is the problem this field exists to answer.

x-accepted-values.test: identity_oidc::discovery::tests::jar_is_declined_explicitly_rather_than_omitted asserts all three boolean fields are false

request_parameter_supported.description: Whether this provider will accept a request with no redirect_uri — that is, whether the redirect target may be learned from the request. Always false: a redirect URI learned at request time is the open redirect this design refuses.

require_request_uri_registration.description: Whether request and request_uri are supported. False: JAR is a large surface and nothing here needs it.
